name: Modern Pop
blurb: From Mariah to Billie: the hit makers and happy accidents of modern pop.

stories.title: The Swedish Hit Factory
stories.dek: How a Stockholm studio taught radio how to build a pop song
stories.body:
In the early 1990s a small Stockholm studio called Cheiron became the quiet engine room of world pop. Its founder, a DJ turned producer who called himself Denniz PoP, had a feel for hooks that were bright, simple and impossible to forget. Working with him was a young musician named Karl Martin Sandberg, who had sung in a Swedish hard-rock band called It's Alive. He took the name Max Martin, and he and PoP began writing songs together.

The sound they built was careful and cold-eyed. Martin has described writing melodies first and fitting words to them afterward, sometimes picking syllables for how they felt in the mouth rather than for meaning. That habit helps explain why lines from their songs stick even when the words are odd. Their studio also worked quickly, turning out demos that singers could learn in an afternoon.

Cheiron's early hits came from acts such as Ace of Base, and then the Backstreet Boys, whose early singles were recorded in Stockholm. Then, in 1997, Martin and his colleague Rami Yacoub worked on a song for a teenage singer from Louisiana. The track was called "...Baby One More Time". The song has often been reported to have been offered to TLC first. Britney Spears sang it in Stockholm, and the record came out in the fall of 1998.

The timing was almost cruel. Denniz PoP, who had been fighting stomach cancer, died in August 1998 at 35, only weeks before the song reached the public. Cheiron wound down by 2000, and Martin carried the sound out of the studio and into the wider world.

Spears's single opened a long run for him. He wrote or co-wrote hits for the Backstreet Boys, NSYNC, Kelly Clarkson, Katy Perry, Pink, Taylor Swift, the Weeknd and many others. The same pattern repeated again and again: a clean beat, a chorus that arrives early and an economy that leaves no room for filler.

Many of those hits borrowed from rock, dance and country, but the method stayed the same. A Swedish studio with a few keyboards and a lot of tape had taught the world's radio stations how a pop song should be built.

stories.title: Adele's 21
stories.dek: A breakup, a piano and the album that won six Grammys
stories.body:
In 2008 Adele was a 19-year-old from London with a debut album, 19, and a gift for sounding older than her years. A few years later she was in the studio with a heartbreak that would make an even bigger record.

She has said that the song "Rolling in the Deep" began on the day after a breakup, when she walked into a London studio angry. Producer Paul Epworth, who had worked with indie bands before, built a pounding beat while she sang in a low, furious voice. They have said the core of the song came together quickly, and the finished record kept its stomping drum and gospel shout of a chorus.

Her new album, named 21 for her age, was shaped by the same breakup. It was recorded in several places, with different producers, including Rick Rubin, who helped on some tracks. Rubin has been known for stripped-down work, and several songs on the album have little more than piano, guitar and her voice. The ballad "Someone Like You" was written with Dan Wilson, who earlier led the band Semisonic, after she learned that her former partner had moved on. At the 2011 BRIT Awards she sang it at a piano with no band, and the song surged up the charts in the days afterward.

Adele was not a typical star. She relied on her voice and a plain-spoken manner, and the album stayed on charts around the world for years. Then her voice failed her. In late 2011, after a hemorrhage on a vocal cord, she cancelled tour dates and had surgery. When she returned at the 2012 Grammy Awards, she sang "Rolling in the Deep" and won six awards for the album and its songs, including Album of the Year.

The result was a record about a private heartache that millions of listeners took for their own, and one more proof that a plain voice and a good song can still beat the biggest production.

stories.title: Believe and Auto-Tune
stories.dek: The robotic voice that came from a seismic engineer
stories.body:
In 1998 Cher was 52 years old and had been famous for more than three decades. She was an unlikely star for the dance clubs of the new decade. But her label gave her a new song, "Believe", and a pair of British producers, Mark Taylor and Brian Rawling, who had an idea.

The song was written by several people, including members of a British songwriting group. When the producers recorded Cher's vocal, they ran it through a piece of software called Auto-Tune. The program had come out in 1997 and was meant to be invisible, quietly nudging a singer's off-key notes into place. Taylor and Rawling instead pushed the setting to its extreme, so that her voice jumped from note to note in a robotic step. The effect was strange and exciting, and it sounded like nothing else on radio.

The software's creator was an engineer named Andy Hildebrand, who had come to music from the oil business, where he analyzed seismic data. The same math could find the pitch of a voice, and he built it into a plug-in.

The producers were worried that other studios would copy the sound, so they said, for a time, that they had used a vocoder or a similar device. Cher also faced doubts from her label, which reportedly asked for a different treatment. She is said to have refused, telling executives that the song should stay as it was. The record came out in the fall of 1998 and became a hit in dozens of countries.

Soon, other singers were using the effect on purpose. In the years that followed, hip-hop and R&B singers such as T-Pain turned it into a style. By the 2010s Auto-Tune was everywhere, both as a hidden fix and a creative choice.

For Cher, "Believe" was a second wind. She had helped turn a tool made to hide errors into a new instrument, and a quirk of software became part of pop's sound.
